definition: Postulate means to assume something as a starting point for reasoning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word postulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know postulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Euclid postulated that parallel lines never meet, then built two thousand years of geometry on the assumption.
A guess is weaker than a postulate — no structure, no plan, nothing built on it — while a postulate is adopted deliberately so reasoning can begin.
Establish goes further than postulate: what you postulate you merely assume for the sake of the argument, while what you establish has been proven.

To assume is to take something as true without noticing you have done it — casual, silent, unflagged. Postulate is the same move made openly and on purpose: the assumption is announced so everyone can see what the reasoning stands on. Assuming slips past; postulating is stated method.

To presume is to believe something with more confidence than your evidence has earned, and to act as if it were settled. Postulate claims no belief at all: a postulated rule is adopted openly as a working basis, while a presumption quietly overreaches toward certainty.
to establish with evidence, so nothing is assumed
to withhold acceptance until the evidence arrives

Postulate comes from Latin postulare, “to demand or claim” — later, “to claim as a basis for argument.” Outside this word and its noun twin, the root left almost no trace in English: its only cousin, postulant (a person formally requesting entry into a religious order), is rare. There is nothing here to peel off and reuse.
Postulate means to assume something as a starting point for reasoning.
Search planners postulate that a lost hiker drifts downhill and toward water.
The rule is openly imperfect — some hikers climb — but adopting it lets the team rank the map's sectors within minutes instead of arguing all night.
Postulate is exact because the team did not claim the rule was true; they assumed it, deliberately and in the open, so reasoning could start.
That is the word's whole job — a stated starting point.
Posit would offer the rule for debate; postulate puts it to work.
Postulate is at home in mathematics and science, where an assumption is adopted openly so reasoning can proceed.
Posit, its neighbor in this unit, offers a claim for discussion; postulate installs one as a foundation.
In casual speech, assume covers both.

Nineteenth-century physics had a problem: light behaved like a wave, and every wave anyone knew needed something to wave through.
So the field postulated a medium -- the 'luminiferous ether' -- an invisible substance filling all of space.
Nobody claimed to have touched it.
The ether was adopted openly, as a starting point: grant this one substance, the textbooks said, and the rest of optics follows.
Because the premise was stated rather than smuggled, it could be tested -- and in 1887 a famous experiment went looking for the ether's effects and found none.
The theory fell, but the method worked exactly as intended.
A starting point laid on the table can be examined, attacked, and finally removed.
One nobody notices cannot.
